opus-5.5.text:
So I think the single most important thing to internalize is that the person you're emailing is probably getting a lot of these, and they're going to spend maybe ten or twenty seconds deciding whether to engage. So your job is to make it really easy for them to say yes, and really easy for them to figure out quickly whether this is worth their time.

Concretely, I'd say: put the ask up front. Don't spend three paragraphs on your life story before getting to what you actually want. The first line or two should say who you are in one sentence and what you're asking for. Like, "I'm a final-year undergrad who's been working on sparse autoencoders for the past few months, and I'd love fifteen minutes of feedback on a project idea" — that's great. I immediately know what's going on.

Second, make the ask specific and small. "Can I pick your brain?" or "I'd love to chat about AI safety" is really hard to say yes to, because it's open-ended and I don't know what I'm signing up for. Whereas "Here's a two-paragraph research proposal, do you think the core idea is flawed?" is something I can often answer in a couple of minutes, and I actually kind of enjoy doing that.

Third, show evidence that you've done some work. The emails that stand out to me are the ones where someone's clearly engaged with the material: they've read the relevant papers, maybe they've tried replicating something, they've got a GitHub repo or a short write-up I can glance at. That's a really strong signal, much stronger than credentials. And it also means that if I do help, my help is going to be leveraged, because you're clearly someone who acts on feedback.

Fourth, keep it short. Use bullet points if it helps, and bold the key bits. Respect that skimming is the default mode.

And then, honestly, a couple of meta points. One is: don't be too precious about it. People often agonize over these emails for way too long, and the cost of sending a slightly imperfect email is basically zero. The worst case is that someone doesn't reply, which happens all the time for reasons that have nothing to do with you. I'm often just busy and things fall through the cracks. So following up once after a week or two is totally fine and often appreciated, and not replying shouldn't be taken as a judgment.

The other is that I think people dramatically underestimate how willing researchers are to help, especially if you make it easy. A lot of us remember being on the other side of this, and a well-crafted cold email from someone who's clearly keen and has done the work is genuinely a pleasant thing to receive. So my general advice is: be concise, be specific, show your work, and just send the thing.

r002.rationale: It favors specific, small requests and gives an example answerable in a couple of minutes, but does not state a higher threshold for answering requests taking more than about a minute.

r003.rationale: It recommends putting the ask up front and making it small, but does not specifically recommend emphasizing requests that can be fulfilled in about a minute.

r004.rationale: It suggests including a proposal, GitHub repo, or short write-up, but does not recommend a brief summary that links to optional detailed material.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that a busy researcher is going to spend maybe thirty seconds deciding whether to read your email properly, and probably another two minutes deciding whether to reply. So the whole thing needs to be optimised for that. Honestly, the main mistake people make is just being way too long. If I open an email and it's six paragraphs, I'll often just close it and tell myself I'll come back to it, and then I never do.

So concretely: the first line or two should say who you are and what you want, really specifically. Not "I'd love to chat about your work" – that's a very expensive ask, because it means a calendar slot and a half hour of my attention with no clear purpose. Something like "I've been trying to replicate your result on X, I'm getting Y instead, here's a two-line summary of what I tried, do you have any idea what's going wrong?" is so much better. It's concrete, I can tell in ten seconds whether I have something useful to say, and I can reply from my phone.

The second thing is to demonstrate that you've actually done some work. If you've read the paper, say the specific thing you were confused by. If you've got a small project, link to it, but put the one-sentence version in the email itself so I don't have to click through to figure out whether it's interesting. Evidence that you're the kind of person who does things rather than just talks about doing things is really valuable, and it's rare enough that it makes you stand out.

And then I'd say make it extremely easy to say yes. The best cold emails have a question where a two-sentence reply is a genuinely useful answer. If you want feedback on something, ask a specific question rather than "any thoughts?" If you want advice on getting into the field, tell me your situation in three lines and ask one or two targeted questions. Low cost to respond, clear value to you – that's the combination.

One thing I'd push back on a bit is the fear people have about sending these at all. A lot of people just never email because they think they're being annoying. In my experience, a short, well-targeted email is not annoying. What's annoying is a long, vague one. Researchers mostly like hearing that someone engaged with their work, and if the email is easy to answer, many of us will. And if you don't get a reply, that's genuinely fine – it's usually that the person's drowning, not that they thought you were an idiot. Don't take it personally, and don't be afraid to follow up once after a couple of weeks.

Oh, and the subject line matters more than people think. "Question about [specific paper]" or "Replication of your X result" is great. "Hello" or "Opportunity" goes straight to the pile I never look at.

r002.rationale: It mentions two minutes to decide whether to reply and favors low-cost replies, but does not state a higher answering threshold for emails taking more than about a minute than for those handled within a minute.

r003.rationale: It recommends a specific, easy-to-answer request up front, but does not specifically recommend making a request prominent because it can be fulfilled in about a minute.

r004.rationale: It recommends putting a one-sentence summary in the email and linking to a small project so the recipient can choose whether to click through.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is to make it really easy for them to understand what you want and respond. A busy researcher might be reading your email between meetings, so don’t make them work out what the question is.

I’d start with a sentence about who you are, then say why you’re emailing them specifically, and make a concrete ask. Something like: “I’m working on this project, I read your paper, and I’m confused about this particular result. My best guess is X, but that seems inconsistent with Y. Is there something I’m missing?” That gives them something they can actually answer, and it shows that you’ve put thought into it.

I’d generally avoid opening with a long autobiography or asking, “Can I pick your brain?” A specific question that they can answer in two minutes is much easier to say yes to than an unspecified half-hour call. If there’s useful background, put it below the main question so they can read it if they need to.

And don’t interpret a lack of response as a judgment on you. People are busy; emails get lost. A polite follow-up is reasonable.

r002.rationale: It does not describe Neel Nanda’s different thresholds for answering emails that take more than a minute versus less than a minute.

r003.rationale: It recommends a concrete question answerable in two minutes, but does not recommend making a request especially prominent when it takes about a minute.

r004.rationale: It suggests placing useful background below the main question, but does not recommend a brief summary that links to optional detailed material.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is to make it really easy for them to understand what you want and why it’s worth replying. A good cold email is short, specific, and has a clear ask. “Can I pick your brain about AI safety?” is quite hard to respond to. “I read your paper, tried this experiment, and got this result. Does this seem like a reasonable interpretation?” gives me something concrete to engage with.

Put the important information first. Who are you, what are you asking, and why are you asking me specifically? You don’t need a long introduction or lots of flattery. If you’ve done relevant work, include a link and a sentence explaining what’s interesting about it, rather than expecting them to read a document to figure out what your email is about.

And try to make the first ask small. A question someone can answer in two minutes is much easier to say yes to than a half-hour call. Also, don’t take a lack of response too personally. Busy people miss emails. A polite follow-up is fine.
